content: Cervical cancer screening and treatment strategies are evaluated based on diagnostic test accuracy, patient outcomes, and resource implications. The effectiveness of different screening methods, such as HPV testing, cytology (ASCUS), and colposcopic impression, is assessed using sensitivity and specificity metrics. For example, pooled sensitivity for HPV testing is 94% (95% CI: 89–97), while its specificity is 90% (95% CI: 86–93). Cytology (ASCUS) has a pooled sensitivity of 70% (95% CI: 57–81) and specificity of 95% (95% CI: 92–97). Colposcopic impression demonstrates a high sensitivity of 95% (95% CI: 86–98) but a low specificity of 42% (95% CI: 26–61). The quality of evidence (QoE) for these outcomes is considered very low due to limitations in study design, indirectness, inconsistency, and imprecision. This low confidence stems from the poor quality of evidence regarding treatment effects and the natural progression of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer. Mortality from cervical cancer is estimated at 250 deaths per 350 women diagnosed with the disease. The incidence of cervical cancer is based on an age-standardized rate of 350 cases per 100,000 women in Eastern Africa, with 2% of women having CIN2+ lesions. Of these, 30% regress naturally, leaving 14,000 women with persistent CIN2+. In untreated cases (true negatives and false negatives), no cervical cancer or CIN2+ is assumed. For false negatives, calculations are based on a 70% persistence rate of CIN2+ without treatment, with 30% regression. Mortality and cancer incidence are subtracted from the persistent CIN2+ cases. Major bleeding is assumed to be absent in untreated cases (true negatives and false negatives). However, 0.001705 of the population treated with cold knife conization (CKC) is expected to experience major bleeding, based on pooled proportions from observational studies. Similarly, premature delivery is estimated to occur in 0.001705 of women treated with CKC, with a baseline population risk of 5% for premature delivery in 1% of pregnant women. No data were identified regarding the risk of infertility following treatment for CIN2+. Major infections are assumed to be absent in untreated cases, but 0.000888 of women treated with CKC are expected to develop major infections. Minor infections are also absent in untreated cases, but 0.009368 of women treated with CKC are expected to experience minor infections. Cancers detected during first-time screening are calculated based on data from Sankaranarayanan et al. (2005). For single screening tests, the number of cancers detected includes both screen-detected and clinically detected cases. No cancers are assumed to be found in the no screen group. These calculations reflect the prevalence of cancer at the time of screening rather than the annual incidence. The recurrence of CIN is assumed to be constant across age groups, but the incidence of cervical cancer and associated mortality increases with age, reducing the overall recurrence of CIN. These data are primarily intended for comparisons across screening and treatment strategies rather than within age groups. The expert panel recommends a screen-and-treat strategy using visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) followed by cryotherapy (or LEEP if cryotherapy is not eligible) over cytology followed by colposcopy (with or without biopsy) and treatment with cryotherapy (or LEEP if not eligible). This recommendation is based on fewer harms associated with VIA, despite overtreatment and fewer cancers detected at first-time screening. VIA requires fewer resources compared to cytology programs, which demand increased training, quality control, and additional visits. The evidence for VIA compared to cytology followed by colposcopy is based on pooled sensitivity and specificity data. VIA has a sensitivity of 77% (95% CI: 66–85) and specificity of 82% (95% CI: 67–91), while cytology (ASCUS) has a sensitivity of 84% (95% CI: 76–90) and specificity of 88% (95% CI: 79–93). Colposcopic impression has a sensitivity of 95% (95% CI: 86–98) but a specificity of 42% (95% CI: 26–61). The overall quality of evidence for these outcomes remains very low due to limitations in study design and variability in results. The recommendation for VIA over cytology applies to all women, regardless of HIV status, and is particularly relevant for countries considering either strategy or those with both strategies available. High value is placed on the benefits of screening and immediate treatment, with lower value placed on the associated harms and resource requirements. This transformation maintains the technical details while presenting the information in a clear and professional manner suitable for medical experts.
